content.p: On 29 December 2021 a federal jury in Manhattan found Ghislaine Maxwell, the longtime companion and onetime girlfriend of the financier Jeffrey Epstein, guilty on five of six counts. Prosecutors had charged that she helped Epstein sexually abuse underage girls. On 28 June 2022 she was sentenced to 20 years in prison. Epstein died in a New York jail in 2019, before his own trial on sex trafficking charges, in a death ruled a suicide. NBC News has called Maxwell the only other person charged and convicted in connection with him.

Her convictions have survived every challenge so far. A federal appeals court affirmed them in September 2024, the Supreme Court declined to hear her case on 6 October 2025, and on 25 August 2026 a judge rejected, as "demonstrably meritless", a petition in which she said her trial had been unfair. In between, she was moved to a minimum-security prison camp in Texas after a long interview with the Justice Department's second-in-command, refused to answer questions from a House committee, and became the subject of an open argument over whether President Donald Trump might pardon her. In late August 2026 she was serving her sentence at Federal Prison Camp Bryan in Texas.
content.h2: Epstein's death and an arrest in New Hampshire
content.p: The Associated Press dated the first public allegations against Epstein to 2005. In Florida he admitted sex offences and spent 13 months in jail, much of it on work release, under a deal critics found lenient. In that 2007 arrangement the United States agreed not to charge "any potential co-conspirators of Epstein", a phrase that would matter again years later. Federal prosecutors in New York took up the case after the Miami Herald's reporting in 2018 and arrested Epstein in July 2019. The following month he was found dead in his cell.

Maxwell was arrested eleven months after his death. FBI agents took her into custody at about 8:30 a.m. on 2 July 2020 at a 156-acre property in Bradford, New Hampshire, which prosecutors said she had bought for about $1 million in late 2019 through an anonymous company. The indictment unsealed that day carried six counts, among them conspiracy, enticing a minor to travel for illegal sex acts, transporting a minor and two counts of perjury over a 2016 deposition. "Maxwell was among Epstein's closest associates and helped him exploit girls who were as young as 14 years old," Audrey Strauss, then the acting US attorney in Manhattan, said at a news conference.

Maxwell pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors called her a flight risk, noting that she held three passports and assets of more than $20 million, and she was held without bail for the 16 months before her trial. The second superseding indictment of 29 March 2021 held eight counts, and six of them went to the jury. The two perjury counts were severed from the trial and dismissed at sentencing.
content.h2: Four and a half weeks in court
content.p: The trial began on 29 November 2021 and lasted about four and a half weeks, according to the Second Circuit, which later wrote that the government had presented evidence of repeated sexual abuse of six girls. Four women took the stand and said they had been abused as teenagers in the 1990s and early 2000s, at Epstein's houses in New York, Florida and New Mexico and in the Virgin Islands. Three were known in court only by a first name or pseudonym: Jane, Kate and Carolyn. The fourth, Annie Farmer, used her own name.

Maxwell's lawyer Bobbi Sternheim told jurors in her opening statement that the case was "about memory, manipulation and money". The defence pointed to gaps in the accusers' earlier statements, noted what each had received from the Epstein victims' compensation fund, and portrayed Maxwell as an associate turned scapegoat after Epstein's death. Maxwell did not testify. She said she saw "no reason" to defend herself formally because the government had not proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt.

The jury convicted her on two conspiracy counts, one over enticing minors to travel for illegal sex and one over transporting them for sexual activity that would be a crime, and on the transport of a minor for that purpose, on a sex trafficking conspiracy, and on the sex trafficking of a minor. It acquitted her on the count of enticing a minor to travel. The five counts carried a combined maximum of 65 years. "We firmly believe in Ghislaine's innocence," Sternheim said afterward, adding that the defence had already started work on an appeal.

On 28 June 2022 Judge Alison Nathan sentenced her to 240 months, with five years of supervised release and a $750,000 fine. Prosecutors had asked for 30 to 55 years and the defence for no more than five. At the hearing the judge told the court that "a very significant sentence is necessary" and said she wanted to send an "unmistakable message". Prosecutor Alison Moe argued that Maxwell and Epstein "were partners in crime together and they molested these kids together". Maxwell, who denies abusing anyone, told the court it was the "greatest regret of my life that I ever met Jeffrey Epstein" and called him "a manipulative, cunning and controlling man". Prosecutors called her shifting of blame to him "absurd and offensive". Annie Farmer told the court, "we will continue to live with the harm she caused us."
The appeals court later recorded that the judgment ran concurrent terms of 60, 120 and 240 months.
The Second Circuit, in an opinion by Judge José Cabranes for a three-judge panel, rejected her appeal on 17 September 2024.

The first concerned Epstein's deal. Her lawyers argued that the promise not to charge his "potential co-conspirators" protected her too. The court held that Epstein's agreement with prosecutors in southern Florida did not bind the office in the Southern District of New York, since its text limited its scope to southern Florida and nothing showed the New York office had been told of it or had approved it. It also held that the indictment was timely, because a 2003 amendment extended the time to bring charges of child sexual abuse, including for conduct from before the amendment took effect.

The second concerned a juror, called Juror 50 in the record. On the written questionnaire he had answered "no" when asked whether he or anyone close to him had been a victim of sexual abuse or assault. After the verdict he told journalists that he was a survivor of childhood abuse. At a hearing on 8 March 2022, under a grant of immunity, he testified that his answers had been an inadvertent mistake that did not affect his fairness. Judge Nathan found him credible and refused a new trial; the Second Circuit held that this was not an abuse of discretion. The panel also rejected her arguments about the judge's reply to a jury note and about the reasonableness of the sentence, and rehearing was denied on 25 November 2024.

Her lawyer David Oscar Markus then took the non-prosecution argument to the Supreme Court. Solicitor General D. John Sauer replied that under internal policy the US attorney would have needed his superiors' permission for the deal to reach beyond his district, and that there was no evidence he got it. On 6 October 2025 the justices declined to hear the case, without giving reasons. Markus said the "fight isn't over". Asked about a pardon that day, Trump said "I haven't heard the name in so long" and that he would "have to take a look".
content.h2: An interview, then a move to Texas
content.p: In July 2025 Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche met Maxwell for nine hours over two days. NBC News called the meeting an unusual twist, noting that Blanche had previously been a personal lawyer for Trump, and a senior administration official told the network that she had been given limited immunity. Markus said there were "no asks and no promises" about clemency. In transcripts the Justice Department released later, Maxwell said she had never seen Trump behave inappropriately.

About a week after the interview she was moved from the low-security prison in Tallahassee, Florida, to the camp at Bryan. A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson confirmed the move to Newsweek. Yahoo News later reported that the Justice Department denied any connection between the interview and the move. NBC News reported that current and former bureau employees condemned the move, calling it very unusual for a prisoner with a sex-offence record and saying it indicated preferential treatment.

Accusations of special treatment followed. NBC News, citing a Wall Street Journal report, described accommodations for her visitors, meals taken to her room and late-night workouts. Representative Jamie Raskin wrote to the warden in October 2025, and emails Maxwell sent from Bryan were shared with the House Judiciary Committee. "My situation is improved by being at Bryan," she wrote in one. In another she said she was "much much happier here and more importantly safe". Markus called the publication of her private emails "tabloid behavior". Staff from two House committees visited the camp in mid-June 2026 and afterward accused the bureau of shutting down basic questions.

The Epstein Files Transparency Act became law on 19 November 2025. Judge Paul Engelmayer, who had by then taken over the case, had refused on 11 August 2025 to unseal Maxwell's grand jury records, finding that each of the two grand juries had heard evidence on a single day and that, with minor exceptions, the material was already public. On 9 December, holding that the new law overrode the grand jury secrecy rule, he granted the department's motion to release that material and the trial discovery, with a mechanism to protect victims' identities. On 21 January 2026 he rejected a request from Representatives Thomas Massie and Ro Khanna to take part in the case and ask for an independent monitor of the department's compliance, writing that a criminal case gave him no authority over a civil records statute.

On 9 February 2026 Maxwell appeared by video from Texas for a closed-door deposition with the House Oversight Committee. She repeated that she was invoking "my Fifth Amendment right to silence". Markus told the committee she was "prepared to speak fully and honestly if granted clemency by President Trump" and that Trump and Bill Clinton "are innocent of any wrongdoing". Committee chairman James Comer said he opposed immunity or clemency for her of any kind, and Democrats accused her of campaigning for clemency. Relatives of the late Virginia Giuffre, one of Epstein's most outspoken accusers, wrote to Maxwell that she was "a central, deliberate actor in a system built to find children, isolate them, groom them, and deliver them to abuse".

On 17 December 2025 Maxwell, acting without a lawyer, asked the court under 28 U.S.C. section 2255 to set aside her conviction. She argued that evidence had been withheld, that witnesses had lied, that lawyers for Epstein's victims had acted as "de facto prosecutors", and that she had been singled out in his place. In an amended petition in April 2026 she cited documents released under the new transparency law.

Engelmayer ruled on 25 August 2026 in 67 pages, working through what he called her "10 principal claims" and denying the petition without the hearing she sought. He found her claims "all meritless and all or almost all are frivolous", and MS NOW reported that he treated most as procedurally barred because she had raised them on direct appeal or could have. The "new" evidence she pointed to, principally the released files, was in his words "largely irrelevant to the charges against Maxwell" and "does not support her claims of error"; "to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges". He called the case "the epitome of a virtuous prosecution". He also declined to certify the case for appeal and refused her leave to appeal without paying costs, writing that "Any appeal from this order would not be taken in good faith".

Two days later Maxwell's family called the ruling "disappointing and shocking" and said it showed "a tone of sarcasm and disdain". They said "our sister is not going to let the matter rest" and that they were encouraging her to apply for a certificate of appealability so that the Second Circuit could review the case.

In November 2025 Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that he had not thought about a pardon for months and added, "I don't rule it in or out". In February 2026 the White House pointed to earlier remarks suggesting a pardon was not on his radar. At the end of July 2026 the Senate unanimously passed a resolution by Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada stating that Maxwell "should not be granted a Presidential pardon or any form of clemency". The resolution has no binding force.
